title: Not a better wrestler
hook: someone may out-wrestle you, but not be kinder or more modest (Meditations 7.52)

segments.voice: Yesterday: vine, the quiet click of doing the fitting thing. Your line was content with right. Did you enjoy one unnoticed good? Day five hundred ninety-three.

There's always someone better. Better at your job, better at tennis, better-looking, better paid, better at small talk. Your cousin got the promotion. Your old classmate wrote the book. The comparison machine never runs out of fuel, because there's always another name to feed it. Marcus Aurelius didn't try to smash the machine. In book seven he used a picture from the wrestling ground to switch it to a different contest entirely.
screen: `THERE'S ALWAYS SOMEONE BETTER.` → `THE COMPARISON MACHINE.` → `A DIFFERENT CONTEST.`

segments.voice: First, the concession. In Meditations seven, fifty-two, Marcus admits it plainly: someone else may be better at throwing an opponent. He doesn't pretend otherwise. Some people really are more talented than you at things. Second, the list. But, he says, that person is not more devoted to the common good. Not more modest. Not better trained to meet whatever happens. Not more considerate of other people's faults. Four contests, and none of them depends on your body, your luck, or your talent. Third, the switch. Here's what Marcus is doing. He doesn't kill the urge to compete. He moves it. If you're going to try to outdo people, outdo them in the things that are entirely in your power. You can't choose to be taller or quicker. You can choose to be more patient with a coworker's mistakes. And in that contest, anyone can win, and nobody has to lose. Fourth, the trick hiding inside it. When you compete in kindness, the other person benefits from your winning. That's a strange kind of competition. Paul's letter to the Romans has a neighboring line, in the King James words: "in honour preferring one another." Different tradition, with its own reasons and its own meaning. So the next time the comparison machine starts up, let it. Then ask it a different question. Not who's better. Who's kinder, today?
screen: `SOMEONE WRESTLES BETTER.` · `NOT MORE MODEST OR CONSIDERATE.` · `COMPETE IN WHAT'S YOURS.` · `A CONTEST WHERE OTHERS WIN TOO.` · then, large: `OUT-KIND THEM.`

segments.voice: Sit, and breathe. Think of someone you tend to compare yourself to. Let the comparison come: they're smarter, richer, more admired. Notice any sting. Now change the contest. Ask, quietly: could I be more patient than them today? More modest? More forgiving of others' mistakes? Pick one. Picture doing it in one real moment. Breathe with that. The bell holds the time.
Mat. Someone else may beat you there, Marcus admits, but no one can stop you being kinder or more modest. Today's word.
Your line: out-kind them. When the comparison machine starts today, compete in kindness instead. Find one way to be more patient than you have to be. Day five hundred ninety-three.

howItsDone: Readers of Marcus sometimes redirect envy into a contest of character, asking who can be most patient or considerate in a situation rather than who is most talented.

alongside being social, modest and ready for whatever happens.

fork.setup: your cousin got the promotion you wanted, and the envy stings. what's Marcus's move?
options: work out how to beat them next time.
compete instead in patience, modesty and kindness.
fork.reveal: Meditations 7.52: someone may throw an opponent better, but not be more modest or more considerate. Compete there.

trapdoor: what you thought: don't compare yourself to others.
what it means: let the urge to compete run, but point it at kindness and modesty, contests entirely in your power.
what a scholar hears: 7.52's first item is being koinōnikos, social or community-minded, so the contest starts with the common good before modesty or patience.
recall: the ruling part, the steering center

notes: Editor review (y2 pass): Romans 12:10 had been given in modern-translation wording ('outdo one another in showing honor'); now quoted from the KJV and cited, without claiming Paul and Marcus share one insight. Cut the claim that Marcus felt envy, the unsourced note on wrestling in his world, the 'favorite words' superlative, and 'most patient person in the room' (also day 594's review).

Meditations 7.52 paraphrased: another may be more expert in throwing his opponent, but not more social, nor more modest, nor better disciplined to meet all that happens, nor more considerate of the faults of neighbors. Confirm.
Romans 12:10 is paraphrased ('in honour preferring one another' in the KJV); the script says 'outdo one another in showing honor' as a paraphrase. A Christianity Keeper may prefer the KJV wording.
koinōnikos as one of Marcus's frequent words: confirm.
